cards.q: What is speed on an Ethernet port, and how is it negotiated?
cards.a: Speed is the line rate of an Ethernet port. It is negotiated on copper, fixed on fiber, and constrained by the cable category or optics installed. A slow port is usually a mismatch, cabling, or bottleneck rather than the nominal rate.

cards.q: List the standard Ethernet speed ladder from 10 Mbps to 400 Gbps with typical media.
cards.a: 10 Mbps 10BASE-T on Cat3; 100 Mbps 100BASE-TX on Cat5 (2 pair); 1 Gbps 1000BASE-T/-SX/-LX on Cat5e or MM/SM; 2.5 Gbps 2.5GBASE-T on Cat5e/Cat6; 5 Gbps 5GBASE-T on Cat6; 10 Gbps 10GBASE-T/-SR/-LR/-ER on Cat6a or optics; 25 Gbps 25GBASE-* on SFP28; 40 Gbps 40GBASE-* on QSFP+; 100 Gbps 100GBASE-* on QSFP28; 400 Gbps 400GBASE-* on OSFP or QSFP-DD.

cards.q: How do copper and fiber ports negotiate speed?
cards.a: Copper ports advertise capability and the highest common rate becomes the negotiated speed, with forced settings overriding. Fiber ports have no speed negotiation (1G SFP and 10G SFP+ are fixed), though some QSFPs auto-negotiate Ethernet rates via 802.3 AN.

cards.q: What is breakout and how is it used?
cards.a: Breakout splits one high-speed port into several lower-rate links, such as 40G into 4x10G or 100G into 4x25G, using DAC and a splitter. It is a data center staple.

cards.q: Why is link speed not equal to throughput?
cards.a: Link speed (line rate) is not throughput. TCP window, latency, MSS, and drops cap real performance, and the weakest link in a path sets the end-to-end rate, so a 100 Mbps uplink limits a gigabit campus flow.

cards.q: What does auto-negotiation off on a broken cable cause?
cards.a: With auto-negotiation off on a broken cable, the port falls to the lowest common speed, typically 10 Mbps. This red flag appears in the commonly tested suddenly slow question pattern.

cards.q: What commands configure and verify the negotiated speed of a port?
cards.a: Configure with 'speed 1000' (or auto) and 'duplex full' on the interface. Verify the negotiated reality with 'show interfaces gig0/1 | include Gb/s|Mb/s|Duplex|Speed', 'show interfaces status', and 'show interfaces counters rate'.

cards.q: Should you assume the CLI speed setting is the actual negotiated speed?
cards.a: No. Never assume the CLI speed 1000 is running; always verify with 'show interfaces' to confirm what was actually negotiated.

cards.q: What do NBASE-T speeds of 2.5G and 5G provide?
cards.a: NBASE-T (2.5G and 5G) extends the life of existing Cat5e/Cat6 copper without re-cabling, operating at higher speeds over the same 100 m.

cards.q: If a 1G SFP module is inserted into a 10G port, what speed results?
cards.a: Fiber speed is set by the module, so a 1G SFP in a 10G port stays at 1G. A wrong module (for example SX versus LX) is a common silent failure.

cards.q: When one side has a forced speed, why should you also check the duplex?
cards.a: A forced speed may still allow the link to come up yet operate half-duplex, resulting in a slow but up link. So when one side is forced, verify the sibling duplex setting.
1G and above are full-duplex only. Half-duplex exists only for 100M (and legacy 10M) links.
